units.name: Drone Operator

tier.basis: Trained at the GDF Barracks with no other building needed: his infobox gives tier 1, the Barracks lists him among its tier 1 production, and the registry's tier map puts the GDF Barracks at t1.

cost_band.basis: His multiplayer price since patch 1.9.0, the same in his infobox and in the makers' 1.9.0 notes, is a little over a third of the anchor price of the two main battle tanks and below the low threshold, so very low. StrategyWiki's older, lower price is out of date and would be very low as well (see uncertain).

mobility.notes: On foot. Patch 1.9.0 cut his pace from the Field Scout's to clearly slower, and patch 2.0.0 gave a little of it back because the cut had hurt him more than intended; his infobox still shows the 1.9.0 value. Either way he walks a little slower than the Field Scout, the reference. His drone flies nearly three times as fast as he walks, so it keeps up with him easily.

body.notes: One soldier. His quadcopter Combat Drone, a separate small flier that the game counts as an aircraft, is recorded as his second weapon (armament/1), as the registry note asks for spawned helpers.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the armour map turns the infobox's Infantry type into unarmoured. His resistances match the Field Scout's: rifle fire hits him in full, while rocket and cannon damage lose most of their force. As standard infantry he drops prone under sustained fire at low health, taking half damage but stuck in place until the shooting stops or he is ordered to move, and medium and heavy vehicles can run him over. His drone has a small health pool of its own and halves explosive and fire damage.

sensors.notes: His infobox sight is a little under three quarters of the Field Scout's, just inside the medium band. His drone sees a little further than he does, and flown by hand it can look over cliffs and uncover high ground for his side. Like every soldier he spots hidden enemies standing right beside him (a game-wide rule); he has no Detection perk.

armament.name: .45 Hand Cannon
armament.summary: His own sidearm, listed first on his page: an anti-tank pistol that his Codex entry presents as a backup handgun for when the drone is knocked out. It fires single shots of Cannon damage, armour-piercing by the damage map, at a steady pace and reaches a little past the Field Scout's rifle, at ground targets and at aircraft alike. Soldiers resist most of its damage, so vehicles are its targets. Hotfix Update #8 (patch 1.6.0) made it hit a third harder, a change to his own damage rather than the drone's. Hitscan is the family default; no source says how its shots travel.

armament.name: Combat Drone (ATAS Micromissiles)
armament.summary: A Combat Drone, a small quadcopter that flies beside him; his Drone Factory perk replaces it when it is lost (abilities/1). In its default Autonomous mode it trails him and attacks whatever he attacks, two micromissiles to a volley. Their damage type is Rocket, armour-piercing by the damage map; the drone's own page labels them for use against both aircraft and surface targets and rates them good against vehicles, structures and fliers, while soldiers resist most of their damage. It fires only at what his side can already see. The missiles reach nearly two thirds as far as the Field Scout's rifle, measured from the drone, which flies on its own and outpaces any soldier; in Remote Control mode it ranges further out (modes/0). It is an aircraft with a small health pool, so anti-air weapons can shoot it down, and it dies at once when he dies. When he rides in a transport or sits in a garrison the drone stays outside and keeps fighting, and a Skycrane carrying him picks its targets and replaces it when lost. Side-wide doctrines change it: Manufacturing gives drones about half again their health, faster rebuilding and the Networked bonus against Marked targets, and Ambush Protocols keeps every GDF drone invisible until it attacks (a doctrine stealth the registry leaves off units).

crew.notes: One player is the operator. The drone is not a seat but his weapon; in Remote Control mode the player steers it while the soldier stays planted, close to what the remote crew model describes, but the unit coded here is the soldier himself, organic infantry, which the remote model excludes, so the crew is solo. He takes one infantry place in transports and garrisons like any soldier (game-wide).

abilities.name: Remote Control Drone / Autonomous Drone
abilities.summary: One toggle made of two buttons. Remote Control Drone roots the operator where he stands and gives the player direct control of the drone, which may fly anywhere within a fixed radius of him, a little longer than the Field Scout's rifle reach: over cliffs and rivers that stop soldiers, over high ground to uncover it for friendly artillery, or close enough to strike anti-infantry defences while he stays out of their reach (StrategyWiki). Autonomous Drone ends it: he can walk again, and the drone goes back to trailing him and attacking his targets. If the drone is shot down while flown, control returns to him. No source gives a cooldown or how long the switch takes. Coded as the piloted variant of launch-drones; his rooting is part of that interaction, so deploy-siege-mode is not linked (see uncertain).

abilities.name: Drone Factory
abilities.summary: A perk: whenever his Combat Drone is destroyed, a new one is made by itself after a while and flies out from him at no cost, one drone at a time, until he dies, since his death kills the drone. StrategyWiki suggests spending these free drones to find enemy anti-air before sending your own aircraft. No source gives the delay. The respawning-followers variant of reinforce-squad.

modes.name: Remote Control Drone
modes.summary: The operator cannot move while the player flies his drone by hand anywhere within a fixed radius of him, a little longer than the Field Scout's rifle reach, so its missiles can strike well beyond his own pistol. Switching back with Autonomous Drone frees him to walk and returns the drone to his side. No source says whether his pistol keeps firing while he stands planted.

on_death.notes: In the sources he is simply gone, so the infantry default applies. His Combat Drone dies at the same moment. With the side-wide Triangulation doctrine every GDF soldier who dies leaves a Marking Mine behind; that is a picked power, not his own outcome.

strengths.why: Both his pistol and his drone's missiles deal damage built for vehicles (Cannon and Rocket), and the makers count him among the early anti-tank infantry.
Pistol and drone alike fire at aircraft as well as ground targets, so one cheap soldier answers both tanks and fliers.
His drone stays outside and keeps fighting while he rides in a transport or sits in a garrison, and a Skycrane carrying him even picks its targets.
Planted, he flies the drone by hand to scout over cliffs and rivers, uncover high ground for artillery and hit anti-infantry defences from outside their reach.
A lost drone comes back free after a while, so it can be thrown at enemy anti-air to find it before friendly aircraft go in (StrategyWiki).

weaknesses.why: A frail soldier: little health and no armour, most vehicles can run him over, and sustained fire at low health pins him prone.
Soldiers resist most of the Cannon and Rocket damage both his weapons deal, so he does badly against infantry and in close fights (StrategyWiki).
Slower than the basic rifleman since patch 1.9.0, a cut the makers meant to make him pay more for being caught out of position.
Flying the drone by hand roots him in place, and the drone cannot leave a short radius around him.
Most of his firepower rides on a fragile flier that anti-air fire can shoot down, and the drone dies the moment he does.

countered_by.why: The makers strengthened the Field Scout to beat early anti-tank infantry, naming the Drone Operator, and the Dynasty Guard to kill anti-tank troopers faster; his own weapons do little to soldiers.

His drone is an aircraft: the makers gave the Peacekeeper a little splash so it would deal with GDF drones in mirror matches, and StrategyWiki notes that anti-air sites often shoot the drones down, stripping him of his main firepower.
Part of the same anti-air answer: the makers widened the Operative's Sensor Interference, which briefly keeps fliers from firing on ground targets, to trouble Drone Operators and drone harassment.

counters.why: His anti-tank pistol and Rocket-armed drone are built for vehicles; StrategyWiki rates him strong against them and the makers class him as anti-tank infantry.
Both his weapons reach fliers, and the drone's missiles are rated effective against air units.
Base defences: flying the drone by hand lets him strike anti-infantry defences from outside their reach (StrategyWiki), and its missiles are rated effective against buildings.

combos.why: Riding in a carrier keeps him safe while his drone fights on outside: the makers strengthened the Riot Van partly so it would carry Drone Operators better, and named Skycranes packed with them as a GDF tactic that worked too well.
The same reason: riders cannot shoot out of the van, but his drone stays active above it.
The same reason: a Skycrane picks targets for the drones of the Drone Operators it carries and replaces lost ones.
Comms from units such as the Comms Officer or Comms Rig speeds his movement and fire; the makers slowed him in patch 1.9.0 because Comms-boosted Drone Operators were oppressive.

units.memorable: A cheap anti-tank trooper whose real gun is a missile quadcopter: it fights beside him, keeps shooting while he rides in a van, and on command he plants himself and flies it on a short leash.
units.as_player: A cheap, slow T1 soldier. Left mouse fires your anti-tank pistol, and your drone hovers beside you and fires micromissiles at whatever you shoot, tanks and aircraft alike. Q plants you and hands you the drone to fly within a short leash, to scout over cliffs, light up high ground or hit turrets from outside their reach; Q again lets you walk. A lost drone comes back after a while and dies with you, and soldiers, flamers and anti-air are your problem.

uncertain.note: Assault comes from the generalist step. His build tooltip, copied on the GDF Barracks page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/GDF_Barracks), says he flies a combat drone at aircraft and vehicles but uses no role label, so step 1 names nothing. His pistol, listed first, is the main weapon and has no game bonus (no damage type does more than full damage in this game), and the tooltip ties his job to the drone, another weapon. The makers' notes call him early anti-tank infantry, which counts only for secondary roles. Anti-armour would be the natural primary (fit_notes).

Anti-armour enters at step 1 through the makers' anti-tank infantry wording (cited 20 May 2025 notes); anti-air at step 3 through the drone's label for air targets on the Combat Drone page and the tooltip naming air units as what the drone is flown against. The wiki's GDF Arsenal line (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/GDF_Arsenal), which describes him as a flexible trooper against vehicles and aircraft who also spots, is carried by no official post found in the makers' Steam news back to 2022, so it does not count.

The Combat Drone page calls combat drones uncontrollable, while the Drone Operator page (ability box, voice lines and Codex), StrategyWiki and the build tooltip on the GDF Barracks page all have the operator steering his drone. The official texts (tooltip and Codex) settle it for the operator; the Combat Drone page may mean that drones cannot be selected on their own, as for those of the Drone Command Unit and the Drone Turret, but it does not say so.

Deploy by the toggle-or-deploy tie-break, because the operator cannot move at all while he flies the drone, even though the drone itself moves. Deploy-siege-mode and the deploy-anchor trait were considered and left out: the registry's pattern notes fold a soldier who parks to pilot a drone into launch-drones' piloted variant (see abilities/0/patterns), so linking both would count the parking twice.

Banded short from the micromissiles' listed reach, nearly two thirds of the Field Scout's rifle, measured from the drone. The drone flies on its own and attacks whatever the operator attacks, so its real reach from him is longer: in Remote Control mode a leash a little longer than a rifle shot plus the missiles' own reach. The drone-launcher family's default would be long. The Drone Operator page says the drone outranges basic anti-ground defences, yet the GDF Gatling Turret (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Gatling_Turret) reaches twice as far as the missiles, so that claim likely rests on flying the drone in by hand or on defences that cannot fire at fliers.

The Combat Drone infobox types the micromissiles as Rocket, which the damage map makes armour-piercing (step 4); the drone-launcher family does not list that type, so the break is recorded in atypical.

Drone health: the Combat Drone infobox still gives its multiplayer health from before Hotfix Update #8 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/532116974486947422, patch 1.6.0+53654), which raised it by a tenth, as the page's own changelog also says. The same hotfix made the operator's pistol hit a third harder, a change to his own damage, not the drone's.

Infantry and structures come from the pistol's own wording on his page (it may hit both aircraft and ground units) beside its anti-tank label; soldiers take only a small share of its Cannon damage. Air is listed because the infobox gives it an Air target line, which in this game reaches every flier (registry note), so the anti-air trait follows.

His infobox gives the patch 1.9.0 speed; the cited 2.0.0 notes raise it a little, and speed_raw uses the newer figure. Both put him in the slow band. The 1.9.0 cut and price rise come from the makers' notes of 7 July 2026 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/680754149992699178), which call Comms-boosted Drone Operators oppressive and want them punished harder when caught out of position.
StrategyWiki gives a lower, pre-release price; his infobox and the patch 1.9.0 notes give the current one, which the band uses. Both prices are very low.

The perk's rule, that a destroyed Combat Drone is rebuilt automatically after a while, also comes from the Ability page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Ability); no source gives the delay.

The doctrine effects rest on the Doctrine page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Doctrine, verified for patch 1.9.0), whose Manufacturing and Ambush Protocols entries both list the Combat Drone, and on the Stealth page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Stealth), which puts drones under Ambush Protocols among the units hidden while moving. Manufacturing changes numbers and adds the Networked bonus, which the registry keeps in summaries. Ambush Protocols would give named drones a new effect, which the doctrine rule records as a commander-power ability, but the registry's Stealth note keeps that doctrine's wider stealth off, and it hides the drone, not the operator, so no ability is recorded.

Prone and crushing: the Status effect page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Status_effect) names the Drone Operator among the six soldiers who go prone, and the Unit page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Unit) lists him as standard infantry, which most vehicles can crush; the two agree.

The leash comes from the ability box on his page, which gives it in build squares; by the Unit page's scale that is a little longer than the Field Scout's rifle reach. No source says whether the pistol fires while he is planted or how long the switch takes.

The Riot Van page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Riot_Van) says riders cannot shoot out but the drones of GDF soldiers such as the Drone Operator stay active above the van, and the Skycrane page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Skycrane) says a Skycrane controls and replaces the drones of the Drone Operators it carries, even inside a carried Riot Van. The makers' notes of 5 August 2025 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/505083956845086898) and 6 October 2025 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/514096230384535253) also name Drone Operator harassment from Skycranes. The Comms entry rests on the 7 July 2026 notes named under mobility/speed.

The anti-air entries rest on the makers' notes of 5 August 2025 (a little splash for the Peacekeeper so it copes with GDF drones in mirror matches) and 6 October 2025 (Peacekeepers struggling against GDF drones; the Operative's Sensor Interference widened to trouble Drone Operators), both linked under combos, and on the Operative page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Operative), whose pulse keeps fliers from firing on ground targets for a few seconds.

launch-drones is linked as the batch brief names it (piloted variant) and as the table in the registry's pattern notes (research/registry-notes/patterns.md) folds piloting a remote drone into it, but a correction at the top of those notes says a remote-piloted drone is the crew model remote, not launch-drones, and the pattern's summary speaks of releasing drones on a key, which he does not do: his drone is always out. Remote is not used for crew because the unit coded is the soldier, organic infantry, which that model excludes (see crew.notes).

fit_notes.wanted: anti-armour
fit_notes.note: The makers call him anti-tank infantry and both his weapons are built for vehicles, but the role steps reach the generalist fallback: his tooltip uses no role label, his main weapon (the pistol, listed first) has no game bonus, and the tooltip ties his job to the drone.

fit_notes.wanted: scout
fit_notes.note: His hand-flown drone scouts over cliffs and rivers and uncovers high ground, but no stock part meets scout's requires (fast speed, long sight, a sensor trait, stealth, a mark or a reveal), so scout is left out; it would rank behind the two roles kept anyway.

atypical.note: The Combat Drone flies on its own and attacks his targets without being aimed, the auto-target case the mount tie-break names for launched drones; the humanoid body lists only mounts a soldier aims himself or that hit all around him.
The infobox types the micromissiles as Rocket, which the registry's damage map makes armour-piercing (damage step 4); the drone-launcher family lists only explosive, kinetic and EMP damage.

units.name: Sentinel

tier.basis: Built at the GDF Vehicle Bay with nothing else required: its infobox gives tier 1, the Vehicle Bay lists it among its tier 1 production, and the registry's tier map puts the Vehicle Bay at t1.

cost_band.basis: Its multiplayer price, the same in its infobox and on StrategyWiki, is about half the anchor price of the two main battle tanks and sits exactly on the low threshold; a price on an edge takes the higher band.

mobility.notes: Wheeled, and by its infobox nearly three times as fast as the Field Scout and nearly twice as fast as the Hunter Tank, the GDF's battle tank; its build tooltip calls it a fast scout and StrategyWiki stresses its very high speed. As a light vehicle it runs over nothing, and heavy vehicles can crush it. Handling is the wheels default.

body.notes: A light scout car carrying one minigun; the makers drew its look from a futuristic Hummer concept. No source read says whether the gun sits in a turret or how exposed its crew is, so the gun-truck body plan is a judgement (see uncertain and fit_notes); the size follows the size examples for cars and armoured cars.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the armour map turns the infobox's Light vehicle type into light. Its health is less than half the Hunter Tank's, a little higher since Hotfix Update #8. Its armour halves rifle, fire and sniper damage and takes a quarter off rockets and explosives; the infobox lists no protection against cannon fire. StrategyWiki notes that it shrugs off anti-infantry fire but cannot stand up to anti-armour attacks.

sensors.notes: Its infobox sight reaches nearly a third further than the Field Scout's, which keeps it in the medium band; the makers raised it in August 2025 to make the Sentinel a more consistent scout, and StrategyWiki praises its view. It has no Detection perk.

armament.name: PG68 Minigun
armament.summary: Its default Anti-Personnel Projectiles: a rotary minigun firing Rifle damage, kinetic by the damage map, at a very quick pace and reaching a little past the Field Scout's rifle, at ground targets and at aircraft. It is good at running down basic infantry, while vehicles shrug off most rifle damage. In multiplayer each attack also Marks its main target (in the campaign it does not): a Marked enemy is worth Intel to the GDF when it is killed, and GDF Networked weapons (the Hunter Tank, Peacekeeper, Drone Mauler and Trebuchet) reach further and hit harder against it. Side-wide doctrines change marking: Boosted Comms lengthens the reach of marking weapons by nearly a third, and Virulent Scanners makes Marked enemies fire more slowly and take more damage; the silence EM Interference adds is abilities/1. Hitscan is the family default; no source says how its rounds travel.

armament.name: Scanner Rounds
armament.summary: The minigun's alternate fire: small-bore scanner rounds fired about half as often as the minigun and reaching a little further, at ground and air targets. Each hit Marks every enemy within a short radius of the target, a little more than one build square, and deals a trifle of Omni damage, the game's type that ignores all resistances. The makers cut that damage in patch 1.1.1 because massed Sentinels were using the rounds as area fire against infantry, to make them the utility tool they were meant to be. Omni has no damage type of its own in our list (fit_notes).
armament.condition: Only after the Marking Projectiles button; it replaces the minigun's anti-personnel fire until Anti-Personnel Projectiles switches back.

crew.notes: Its voice lines and the campaign-only crew upgrades imply a crew, but no player sits in it; it fires one weapon at a time (the scanner rounds replace the minigun's fire), so one player drives and shoots.

abilities.name: Anti-Personnel Projectiles / Marking Projectiles
abilities.summary: One toggle made of two buttons that swap its ammunition. Marking Projectiles loads the scanner rounds (armament/1): little damage, but every enemy in an area around the hit is Marked. Anti-Personnel Projectiles goes back to the minigun's full damage, which in multiplayer still marks its main target. It can drive in either state. The wiki gives Marking Projectiles a recharge time, in the medium band.

abilities.name: EM Interference (doctrine)
abilities.summary: Not stock. Once the GDF player buys EM Interference, the fifth step of the Comms doctrine tree, every enemy that is Marked, by this car's fire among others, is also silenced while the mark lasts. In this game silence shuts off a unit's active and passive abilities; the pages do not say it stops attacks. The Doctrine page names the Sentinel among the markers this applies to.

on_death.notes: The sources show nothing special when it dies, so the default for a crewed vehicle applies.

strengths.why: Very fast for a ground unit: its tooltip calls it a fast scout and StrategyWiki stresses its speed, so it scouts, chases down stragglers and escapes what it cannot fight.

Its fire Marks enemies, one at a time with the minigun in multiplayer or a whole cluster with scanner rounds: each Marked kill earns the GDF Intel, and Networked weapons hit Marked enemies harder and from further.
Its rapid minigun is good at chasing down and killing basic infantry.
Both its weapons fire at aircraft as well as ground targets; StrategyWiki rates it strong against aircraft.
It sees nearly a third further than the Field Scout, and the makers raised its sight to make it a more consistent scout.

weaknesses.why: Thin health and light armour: StrategyWiki calls anti-armour attacks its main weakness, and it has less than half the Hunter Tank's health.
Its minigun's Rifle damage barely hurts vehicles, so it is weak against them (StrategyWiki).
One ammunition at a time: on scanner rounds it does almost no damage, and switching to them has a wait.

countered_by.why: Rocket and Cannon weapons, the kinds made for vehicles, tear through its thin hull; StrategyWiki names anti-armour attacks as its main weakness.
Its rifle-type minigun barely scratches vehicles, so tanks win the head-on fight; StrategyWiki lists vehicles as its weakness.

counters.why: Its minigun is good at chasing down and killing basic infantry; StrategyWiki rates it strong against infantry.
StrategyWiki rates it strong against aircraft, and both its weapons fire at fliers.
Harvesters: the makers made Dynasty Harvester Wheels easier to kill so that drive-by raids, with units such as Sentinels, slow the Dynasty economy and earn the GDF Intel.

combos.why: Networked tanks such as the Hunter Tank hit Marked targets harder and from further, and kill the vehicles the Sentinel cannot; StrategyWiki says the two cover each other's weaknesses and earn Intel on every kill.
The same reason: the Hunter Tank is the Networked tank StrategyWiki pairs it with.
Networked anti-air such as the Peacekeeper reaches Marked aircraft from further and hits them harder, and the Sentinel's weapons can mark fliers.

units.memorable: A very fast scout car that can trade its minigun's bite for scanner rounds which tag a whole cluster of enemies, so each kill pays the team Intel and Networked tanks hit them harder from further away.
units.as_player: A cheap, very fast T1 scout car with a minigun that shreds infantry and can fire at aircraft; in multiplayer each burst tags its target. Q swaps to scanner rounds that barely scratch but tag everything around the hit, so Networked teammates such as Hunter Tanks hit harder and from further and each tagged kill earns Intel. Thin armour: anti-tank fire and tanks are deadly, so tag, spot and run.

Omni, which ignores all resistances, is not in the damage map, so step 5 gives the machine-gun default, kinetic; the explosive exception for area hits needs a family that allows explosive damage. See fit_notes.

Splash rests on the infobox's area figure and on the makers' notes of 20 May 2025 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/536602273129694258), which say massed marking rounds dealt strong area damage to infantry before those notes cut their damage, slowed them and made them Omni.

The mark trait holds in multiplayer only: the Sentinel page and the Status effect page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Status_effect) say the campaign minigun does not mark. The registry codes multiplayer values.

Its weapon box labels the minigun anti-infantry and anti-air; ground vehicles and structures come from the build tooltip's ground targets and the infobox's Ground line, and StrategyWiki shows it weak, not powerless, against vehicles.

The doctrine effects come from the Doctrine page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Doctrine). Boosted Comms and Virulent Scanners only change numbers for the whole side and stay in this summary; EM Interference, which names the Sentinel among the markers whose targets it silences, is recorded as abilities/1.

Anti-infantry enters at step 1 if the cited Hotfix Update #8 wording (a little more versatility in the GDF's anti-infantry and scouting work) is read as naming its job; otherwise at step 3 through the Codex's anti-infantry minigun. Either way it ranks ahead of anti-air (step 3, the weapon box's anti-air label) by the order of the roles list. Raider (step 4: very fast with light armour) comes third and is dropped.
StrategyWiki gives its pre-launch health; the infobox gives the value Hotfix Update #8 set. The class is light either way.
The cooldown comes from the wiki's ability box for Marking Projectiles; no official text gives it.

Crushing follows the Crushing page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Crushing): light vehicles, the Sentinel among them, crush nothing, and heavy vehicles crush light ones.

The Hunter Tank's Networked figures come from its page on the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Hunter_Tank): against Marked targets it reaches about two fifths further and hits about half again as hard.

Reasoned: the Peacekeeper page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Peacekeeper) gives its Networked missiles more reach and damage against Marked aircraft, and the Sentinel's weapons can mark fliers; no source names the pairing.

Rests on the makers' notes of 6 October 2025 (https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1486920/view/514096230384535253), which cut the Harvester Wheel's health so that drive-by harassment pays, with more Intel for the GDF, and name Sentinels and Field Scouts among the units for it.

Recorded under the registry's doctrine rule (a doctrine that gives named unit types a new effect is recorded on each of them, source commander-power), because the Doctrine page lists the Sentinel under it. But the silence belongs to the Marked status itself, whoever applies it: the Status effect page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Status_effect) says the doctrine makes Marked units silenced too, and defines silence as losing active and passive abilities. The merge pass may judge it a side-wide change and drop it.

fit_notes.wanted: a damage type that ignores armour (the game's Omni)
fit_notes.note: The scanner rounds deal Omni damage, which ignores every resistance; no damage type in the list does that, so the family default stands in.

fit_notes.wanted: a scout car or armoured car body with one gun mount
fit_notes.note: A light scout car with one gun and no passenger room, whose gun mount and crew exposure no source describes, fits neither the tank turret nor the troop carrier, and only loosely the exposed gun truck.

fit_notes.wanted: a pattern for shutting off a target's abilities (here through a mark)
fit_notes.note: No registered pattern stops an enemy from using its abilities while leaving it free to move and fire; the weapon trait silence also stops firing, and disable-machine covers only machines hit by electric or EMP effects.

units.name: Shieldmaiden

tier.basis: Built at the Vehicle Bay once a Satellite Uplink carries its Specialist Pod: the Vehicle Bay page lists it under Tier 2 with that requirement, and its own infobox gives tier 2. The wiki counts pod steps as tier 2.5, which the registry keeps in t2. It is not one of the GDF's Support Specialists, so no specialist cap applies to it; it takes ordinary population places.

cost_band.basis: In multiplayer it is paid for in Intel, the GDF's second currency, not in credits. At the registry's estimated rate of credits per Intel point its price comes to about one and a half times the main-battle-tank anchor, inside high and level with the Sniper and the GDF's other tier 2 specialists. Patch 1.3.0 raised its Intel price by a quarter and patch 1.5.0+51028 took it back down; the 2.0.0 notes leave it alone. Campaign prices are ignored.

mobility.notes: An air-cushion craft (infobox movement type Hovering) that ground weapons hit like any vehicle. It moves a little faster than the Field Scout and at about three quarters of the speed of the Hunter Tank, which is the battle tank the GDF fields. Its Hover perk means it sets off no mines and can neither run other units over nor be run over; the page backs this with a lead designer's remark, and the Codex adds that the air cushion makes pressure mines less of a threat to it. Its interference field works only while it stands still (see abilities).

body.notes: The Codex calls it an air cushion vehicle, and the picture on its wiki page shows an armoured hull on a skirted air cushion with a turret on top that holds the laser. No size example covers a hovercraft and no page gives its footprint, so the size comes from the stand-in rule: in the Skycrane's hold it takes as much room as any other vehicle, the Hunter Tank included (see uncertain).

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: its armour type is Light vehicle, which the armour map makes light. One health bar, about two thirds bigger than the Hunter Tank's. Its resistances turn away three quarters of rifle, fire and sniper damage and half of explosive damage, but only a quarter of rocket damage, and the infobox lists none against cannon fire. The GDF's Investment Durability doctrine gives every Intel-priced unit, this one included, a quarter more health; that side-wide change is left out of the class. Mending out of combat at Elite rank is game-wide veterancy, not a self-repair model.

sensors.notes: Its infobox sight is a little more than the Field Scout's, about a seventh more; its laser reaches a little short of it. It has no detection perk.

armament.name: FLASHPOINT Laser
armament.summary: A high-energy laser in the turret that fires in quick pulses. Its infobox target line is Air alone, so it cannot attack anything on the ground. It reaches about one and a half times as far as the Field Scout's rifle, a little short of its own sight. The game types it as Cannon - Laser, and the registry counts every laser as energy damage. Patch 1.1.0 lengthened its reach a little, patch 1.3.0+48710 retimed its shots, and patch 1.9.0 trimmed its damage per shot by a twentieth so that players would lean on its other tools and on mixed armies for air defence.

armament.name: FLASHPOINT Laser (Pinpoint Weaknesses)
armament.summary: The same laser once the GDF owns the Pinpoint Weaknesses doctrine: every GDF laser then hits a fifth harder and leaves what it hits Marked, so an aircraft it shoots gives the GDF Intel if it dies while Marked and takes more from the side's Networked weapons.
armament.condition: Pinpoint Weaknesses, the second step of the GDF's Intel doctrine tree, bought during a match for the whole side: a commander power, not an upgrade of this unit.

crew.notes: One player drives and fires the laser. Its voice lines speak like a crew, which changes nothing.

abilities.name: Deploy Repair Turret
abilities.summary: Each use draws Intel from the side's stock, half the Shieldmaiden's own Intel price. Its onboard factory sets a small Repair Turret down at a spot the player picks. The turret is a temporary structure with a little over half the Shieldmaiden's health that does no fighting; for its short life, twice as long as the button's cooldown, it quickly mends the allied vehicles within about three fifths of the Field Scout rifle's reach, and then its battery is spent. The pages differ on whether it also mends structures or aircraft (see uncertain). The GDF's Efficient Intel doctrine cuts the cooldown of Intel-priced buttons, a side-wide change left out here.

abilities.name: Missile Interference Aura
abilities.summary: A perk, always on, with no button. While the Shieldmaiden stands still it projects a wide interference field, reaching about as far as it can see; enemy units and defences inside it whose weapons are of the game's Rocket type fire at half their usual rate. Other weapons are untouched. The Comms Officer carries the same perk with a smaller field, and the Haywire Turret with one as wide. The patch 1.9.0 notes count the field, with the Repair Turret, among the tools that should carry its air-defence job.

on_death.notes: No page shows crew, a wreck or a blast when it is destroyed; it is simply gone, so this is the default for a crewed machine.

strengths.why: By the official tooltip its laser does heavy damage to aircraft, and the makers' 1.9.0 notes describe it as an air defender so reliable that players picked it without a second thought.
Its laser reaches about one and a half times as far as the Field Scout's rifle, a reach the wiki calls extreme, so it guards a wide stretch of sky.
Its Repair Turret quickly mends the allied vehicles around it, which the Codex presents as part of its real value to commanders.
As a hover unit, enemy vehicles cannot squash it (nor can it crush anything itself).
It sets off no mines, so minefields do not stop it; the Codex credits its air cushion for this.

weaknesses.why: Its only gun, the laser, can attack aircraft alone, so it has no answer to infantry, vehicles or buildings.
Light vehicle armour that blunts rifles, fire and sniper rounds but turns away only a quarter of rocket damage and none of cannon damage, so tanks wear it down despite its large health bar.
Every Repair Turret costs Intel from the side's stock and lasts only briefly before its battery runs out.

countered_by.why: Tanks and other armed ground vehicles can shoot it without reply, since it has nothing that fires at the ground, and their cannon shells meet no resistance in its armour.

counters.why: Its long-reach laser hits any enemy flier hard; the tooltip stresses its anti-air damage and the 1.9.0 notes call it an air defender.

combos.why: It works beside the GDF's armour: the Codex presents its repair gantries as keeping the side's tanks fit for frontline fighting, and while it stands still its field slows the enemy rocket fire turned on them.
The 1.9.0 notes cut its laser so that GDF players mix it with other units for air defence instead of relying on it alone.

units.memorable: A hovercraft whose laser only looks up: it burns aircraft from far off, drops brief repair turrets for nearby tanks and, parked, makes enemy rocket launchers fire at half speed.
units.as_player: You drift behind your own tanks on an air cushion, burning down any aircraft that comes within your long laser reach. Spend Intel to drop a short-lived repair turret where the armour is fighting, and stop moving to spread a field that halves the fire rate of enemy rocket weapons. You cannot shoot anything on the ground, so you depend on your escorts.

No text describes its shape: hull-turret rests on the picture on its wiki page (an armoured hull with a laser turret on top) and on the Codex's air cushion vehicle. Recorded from the Doctrine page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Doctrine, read, not cited, verified at 1.9.0+58877), which lists the Shieldmaiden among the lasers that Pinpoint Weaknesses makes hit harder and mark. The Missile Interference page and the Status effect page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Status_effect, read, not cited) give a flat halving of the rate of fire, while the Ability page's perk text (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Ability, read, not cited) says the effect grows the longer a unit stays in it. The tooltip speaks of missile weapons, the status pages of the game's Rocket weapon type.
Its infobox has no cannon resistance line, read here as none. The wiki leaves some zero values out (the Field Scout's page lists only some of its resistances), but no page says so for this unit.
Reasoned, not named by any page: from its Air-only target line and its resistance table, which has no entry against cannon fire.
Reasoned from the 1.9.0 notes, which ask for mixed armies in air defence without naming the units; other anti-air units are the teammates read into them.

fit_notes.note: deploy-turret needs a device that fights, so the registry's batch r3 note keeps the Repair Turret off it; repair-allies alone does not show that the mending comes from a timed structure the enemy can shoot.

fit_notes.wanted: an always-on aura that slows the fire of one kind of enemy weapon (rocket and missile launchers) around the unit, here only while it stands still
fit_notes.note: leave-hazard-zone is a zone laid on a key, and as a pattern that mirrors the zone weapon trait it is the home for the ability version only. No armour model or sensor trait slows enemy fire; interceptor shoots missiles down instead. Disabler's requires would need such a pattern in the control category.

fit_notes.wanted: a way to mark a weapon change that a commander power (a doctrine) adds
fit_notes.note: The acquired slot speaks of bought upgrades, research and ranks, and only abilities have a source field that can say commander-power, so the doctrine is named in condition.

fit_notes.wanted: a mark that pays out resources when the marked target dies
fit_notes.note: In Tempest Rising a Marked target gives the GDF Intel on death and takes more from Networked weapons, and the pages describe no reveal for the team, which the mark trait includes.

units.name: Line Officer

tier.basis: Trained at the Dynasty Barracks once a Specialist Bureau stands, a tier 2 tech building: the Barracks page lists that requirement and his infobox gives tier 2. He is one of the Dynasty's Support Specialists, and in multiplayer each player may field three tier 2 Support Specialists at once in any mix (Specialist page), so his availability is limited.

cost_band.basis: His multiplayer price in credits is about one and a half times the main-battle-tank anchor, inside high. The Dynasty's Officers doctrine halves the price of its specialists; that side-wide power is left out of the band.

mobility.notes: A little faster than the Field Scout and as fast as the Dynasty Guard; patch 1.2.0 sped him up slightly.

body.notes: A single officer, Major Mykyta Moroz in the fiction.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: his armour type is Infantry, which the armour map makes unarmoured, and the registry reads the class from that label (see uncertain). He takes a quarter less damage from rifles, explosives, fire and sniper rounds and three quarters less from rockets and cannon shells, and his health is more than four times a Field Scout's. As standard infantry he goes prone under heavy fire at low health and can be run over by medium and heavy vehicles (see uncertain). The Dynasty's Body Armor doctrine gives every infantry unit more health, a side-wide change left out here.

sensors.notes: His infobox sight is a little over half the Field Scout's; since patch 2.0.0 his pistol reaches exactly as far as he sees.

armament.name: RLO .50 Model 62 Handgun
armament.summary: A heavy pistol that fires one precise, very heavy shot after a long pause, enough to kill a Field Scout or a Dynasty Guard outright. The game gives it the Sniper damage type, which vehicles mostly resist, so it does little to them; its target line is Ground. Patch 1.4.0 raised its damage by a quarter and made the pause slightly longer, and patch 2.0.0 stretched its reach by about a ninth, to four fifths of the Field Scout rifle's reach, so that he can keep further back from the fighting. The Dynasty's Officers doctrine raises specialists' damage output, a side-wide change left out here.

abilities.name: Inspire Troops
abilities.summary: A timed call: friendly infantry around him become Inspired and move and fire half again as fast, for a little under half the cooldown. Patch 1.2.0 made the boost last two fifths longer. The Codex credits his presence with better cohesion and morale. The Officers doctrine shortens specialists' cooldowns, a side-wide change left out here.

abilities.name: Supervise Crew
abilities.summary: He climbs into a friendly vehicle the player targets and takes direct charge of it, and while he rides it counts as Elite, the top veterancy rank. By the Veterancy page an Elite unit carries the gains of all three ranks: from Hardened, a tenth more armour resistance and a tenth faster fire; from Veteran, about a seventh more damage per shot and sight, with Charge draining off about a third faster on vehicles; from Elite itself, a quarter more health, mending on its own out of combat and another tenth on damage per shot. Only one Line Officer can supervise a given vehicle. If the vehicle is destroyed he is thrown clear alive and returns to the player's control. The Codex names the button Commandeer Vehicle, and the build tooltip speaks of providing a single powerful vehicle.

on_death.notes: An ordinary death leaves nothing behind. He does not die with a vehicle he supervises: he gets out alive when it is destroyed (see abilities).

strengths.why: Inspire Troops makes the infantry around him move and fire half again as fast for a while, one of the two jobs his official tooltip gives him.
Supervise Crew lifts one friendly vehicle to Elite while he rides inside, with more health, damage, resistance and fire rate and mending out of combat, and he comes out alive if it is destroyed.
One pistol shot can kill a basic soldier outright, and the wiki's weapon text calls the pistol devastating against infantry.

weaknesses.why: His pistol fires only after a long pause and deals the Sniper damage type, which vehicles mostly resist, so on his own he cannot hold off vehicles or large groups.
He sees only a little over half as far as a Field Scout, so he finds enemies late and leans on others' sight.
Even after patch 2.0.0 his pistol reaches less far than a basic rifle; the makers lengthened it a little then to keep him further back from the front line and help him survive.

countered_by.why: Vehicles shrug off most of his pistol's Sniper damage, and medium and heavy vehicles can simply run him over.
His pistol attacks ground targets only, so aircraft can hit him without reply.
Massed rifle infantry: his price buys several Field Scouts, whose combined fire kills him long before his slow pistol can thin them out.

counters.why: Unarmed builders and capturers such as the GDF Engineer: one pistol shot kills one, and they cannot shoot back.

combos.why: Inspire Troops speeds up the movement and fire of the infantry around him; his tooltip names boosting nearby infantry as his first job.

Supervise Crew turns one tank or other armoured vehicle into an Elite one while he rides it; his tooltip calls this providing a single powerful vehicle, and the Codex names tanks as the vehicles he joins.

units.memorable: A grizzled major with a slow, heavy pistol who either speeds up the infantry around him or climbs into one tank to make it Elite, and walks away alive when it blows up.
units.as_player: A tough officer with a slow, hard-hitting pistol that drops soldiers one shot at a time. Press Inspire to make the infantry around you move and shoot faster, or climb into a teammate's vehicle to lift it to Elite rank while you ride, jumping clear alive if it is destroyed. Stay behind the front: vehicles barely feel your pistol.

Also the weapon and ability boxes, the Codex text in the Background box (official, mostly lore; it calls the second button Commandeer Vehicle), prose with a lead designer's Discord remarks (the vehicle goes to top rank; one officer per vehicle) and a reference to the old official Dynasty site (he is evacuated when the vehicle dies), and a changelog up to 1.4.0. Its reach predates patch 2.0.0.

The wiki's weapon text calls the pistol devastating against infantry, which would give anti-infantry at step 4 if it were official; as it is not, the primary falls to assault at step 5.

Limited rests on the Specialist page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Specialist, read, not cited): three tier 2 Support Specialists per player in multiplayer, in any mix, the Line Officer among them. His infobox also gives him a specialist place.

Sniper by the small-arms or sniper tie-break, because the game gives the pistol its Sniper damage type and the wiki describes precise, slow shots. The small-arms or machine-gun tie-break says pistols are always small arms, but it settles a different pair; small arms would change only the family.
The Line Officer page still shows the reach from before patch 2.0.0; the official 2.0.0 notes give the longer one, which decides. Both fall in medium.

That one shot kills a Field Scout or a Dynasty Guard compares its damage with the health given on the pages of the Field Scout and the Dynasty Guard on the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Field_Scout and https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Dynasty_Guard, read, not cited), which list no resistance to Sniper damage; ranks and doctrines aside.

Unarmoured by his Infantry label, which the registry says is enough for the class. His resistances are tougher than the Field Scout's against rifle, explosive, fire and sniper damage (Field Scout page, https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Field_Scout, read, not cited), which the soldier rule's clause on a tougher infantry armour attribute could read as light.

The Unit page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Unit, read, not cited) puts him with the standard infantry, all of whom go prone and can be crushed, but the Status effect page names only six prone units, not him. The crushing rule is on the Crushing page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Crushing, read, not cited).
No page says whether he inspires himself.

No page says whether he can leave the vehicle by himself or whether it keeps Elite after he leaves; the Codex says he joins crews for a time. That only one officer fits a vehicle rests on a lead designer's Discord remark the wiki quotes, and that he gets out alive on the old official site the wiki cites. The Veterancy page lists each rank's gains on its own; that Elite holds the lower ranks' gains too is read from its wording of a further damage rise.

All three entries are reasoned, not named by any page: from vehicle resistances to Sniper damage (Hunter Tank page, https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Hunter_Tank, read, not cited), the crushing rules (Crushing page, read, not cited), the Unit page's remark that most vehicles resist rifle and sniper attacks (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Unit, read, not cited), his Ground-only target line, and, for massed infantry, the prices, health and rifle damage on the Field Scout page (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Field_Scout, read, not cited) set against his own.

Reasoned: the Engineer page of the Tempest Rising Wiki (https://tempestrising.wiki.gg/wiki/Engineer, read, not cited) shows an unarmed Engineer whose health is far below the damage of one pistol shot.

fit_notes.note: rally-allies is an aura or a timed call around the buffer, earn-veterancy is rank earned by fighting, and passenger-sets-weapon changes a vehicle's weapon or job, not its rank.

units.name: Voltaic Tank

tier.basis: Only a Machine Shop that has bought the Defender upgrade can build it, and that upgrade needs the Construction Yard's Bastion first; the wiki's infobox puts it at tier 3. No cap of its own: the population limit is shared by every unit.

cost_band.basis: The wiki's multiplayer price is about one and three quarter times the average of the two anchor tanks, inside our high band. No patch note from 1.6.0 to 2.0.1 changes it.

mobility.notes: About a quarter faster than the Field Scout on the wiki's speed figures, and somewhat slower than the GDF Hunter Tank, the anchor battle tank (about seven eighths of its pace, Hunter Tank page). Its Heavy vehicle (Harvester) type lets it run over standard infantry but not heavy infantry or any vehicle, and since patch 1.5.0 nothing can run it over. Each crush slows the crusher for a moment, as for every vehicle. Handling stays pivot, the tracks default.

body.notes: A tracked battle tank whose Codex entry says it carries the biggest Tempest-battery gun a hull of its size can take.

armour.notes: Step 1 decided: the armour_map reads its Heavy vehicle type (tagged Harvester) as heavy. Its six resistances match the Hunter Tank's: rifle, sniper and fire hits do a quarter of their damage, explosive hits half, rocket hits three quarters and cannon hits their full damage. It has about a fifth more health than that tank; patch 1.6.0 cut its health so that it falls more easily to ordinary attacks. Side-wide effects stay off: the Martial Plan gives every unit a little more resistance to rockets and explosives, and the Leading the Charge doctrine about a third more health to Dynasty vehicles.

sensors.notes: The wiki's sight figure is a little over half the Field Scout's, so short. Its cannon reaches well past what it can see, so it needs other units' vision to fire at full reach. It has no detection perk.

armament.name: Voltaic Cannon
armament.summary: A Tempest-powered particle beam. The tank spends a brief moment building charge before every shot, so its fire comes as slow, visible blasts, one every few seconds. Each blast hurts an area and its arcs leap to enemies close to the target, so tightly grouped vehicles suffer most. Voltaic Reaction: a vehicle already in Tempest Overflow dies to the hit outright, whatever its health. The tank lays no Tempest Charge itself: five stacks of Charge from Tempest fields or from teammates' Charge weapons (Matchstick grenades, the Machinist's sensor, Trebuchet shells, the Salvage Center's gun and others) push a vehicle into Overflow (a few weapons, such as the GDF Sniper's shot from stealth, inflict Overflow directly), and units immune to Charge or Overflow, such as harvesters and the Boar Tank, can never be finished this way. Structural Overload: any building it hits is forced to power down for a short time, so defences stop firing, yet the beam barely damages the structure itself. It reaches about a quarter further than the Field Scout's rifle, further than the Hunter Tank's gun against unmarked targets, and fires at ground targets only. Coded tesla for the arcing beam; its damage is armour-piercing because the game types it as Cannon.

crew.notes: One player drives and fires the beam. The sources name no crew.

abilities.name: Tempest Dynamos / Safe Firing
abilities.summary: Two buttons that undo each other, open only while the Dynasty player runs the Martial Plan at a Construction Yard. Tempest Dynamos switches off the cannon's safety limits: the tank fires about half again as fast but loses health steadily for as long as it stays on. Safe Firing returns to the normal rate and stops the drain. Each switch is followed by a moderate wait before the next. Since patch 1.6.0 silencing effects cannot turn Dynamos off. The Empowered Dynamos doctrine also makes the tank take markedly less damage while Dynamos runs, and Energetic Enhancements strengthens the boost.

on_death.notes: The sources show nothing special when it is destroyed, so the default for a crewed vehicle applies. Two doctrines the Dynasty player buys for the whole side change its death: with Manpower and any Plan running it releases an Assault Gunner, and with Minefields it leaves an anti-tank mine.

strengths.why: Voltaic Reaction destroys any vehicle already in Tempest Overflow with one hit, whatever its health, so it finishes armour that teammates or Tempest fields have overloaded.
Its arcs jump between nearby enemies, so clustered vehicles take heavy damage; the 1.6.0 notes said massed Voltaic Tanks had been winning ground fights too easily, and toned them down.
Its harvester-type hull cannot be run over by anything, not even the heavy vehicles that flatten other tanks.
Every hit powers down the building it strikes for a short time, so base defences fall silent while the army closes in; the lead designer offered it as a late-game answer to defences.
Its beam reaches further than the GDF Hunter Tank's cannon does against targets that are not Marked.

weaknesses.why: Its only weapon can target ground units and buildings alone, so it has no way to fight aircraft.
The beam does very little real damage to buildings: it can switch defences off for a moment but cannot level a base by itself.
It sees much less far than its cannon reaches, so without spotters it cannot use its full range.
Patch 1.6.0 lowered its health so that ordinary attacks would counter it more easily; its resistances are no better than a main battle tank's.
Its fire-rate boost exists only while the side runs the Martial Plan, and it eats the tank's own health for as long as it stays on.

countered_by.why: Its cannon cannot target anything in the air, so aircraft can attack it without any answer.
Its armour takes the full force of Cannon hits and most of each Rocket hit, both armour-piercing in our map, and patch 1.6.0 meant it to fall more easily to ordinary attacks.

counters.why: Made to kill vehicles: its arcing blasts punish grouped armour, and any vehicle pushed into Tempest Overflow dies to a single shot.
Its hits power down base defences for a short time, so they stop shooting while the assault goes in, though the buildings themselves take little damage.

combos.why: Its grenades build Tempest Charge on enemy vehicles; once stacked into Overflow those vehicles die to one Voltaic shot. No word-list link names units that build Charge.
His Searchlight Sensor builds Tempest Charge on enemy vehicles, setting up Overflow kills for the tank's beam. No word-list link names units that build Charge.
Works best in numbers: the makers said a massed group won ground battles with ease, which patch 1.6.0 toned down.
Its gun reaches well beyond its own short sight, so a teammate who sees further lets it fire at full range.
An anti-air escort covers its lack of any weapon against aircraft.

units.memorable: A Tempest beam tank whose slow, charged blasts arc through bunched-up armour, shut enemy defences down for a moment and erase outright any vehicle already overloaded with Tempest Charge.
units.as_player: A T3 armour hunter on a slow turret: each shot needs a short, visible wind-up, then the blast arcs across grouped vehicles and instantly kills any that teammates have overloaded with Tempest Charge. Hits also switch enemy turrets off for a moment but barely scratch buildings. When the side-wide plan allows, Q toggles an overdrive: faster fire that slowly burns your own health. You cannot hit aircraft and see less far than you shoot, so stay near spotters and anti-air.

units.name: Tempest Sphere

tier.basis: Like the Voltaic Tank it comes only from a Defender-upgraded Machine Shop, and that upgrade needs the Bastion; the wiki's infobox puts it at tier 3. No cap of its own.

cost_band.basis: Patch 1.7.0 raised its price to about three times the average of the two anchor tanks, well inside our very-high band; no later patch changes it.

mobility.notes: It rolls as one gyroscopically steadied ball (the game's movement type is Roller), which no mobility type names: wheels is the nearest, a ball being one big wheel, and steer is that type's default. About a third faster than the Field Scout on the wiki's speed figures and a little slower than the Hunter Tank, the GDF's anchor battle tank; the Codex calls it somewhat ponderous. As a heavy vehicle it rolls over every soldier, heavy infantry included, and over light and medium vehicles, main battle tanks among them; hover units and heavy vehicles cannot be crushed. Each crush slows it for a moment. The Tempest Engine gives a brief burst of speed on a long wait (boost).

body.notes: A single armoured ball with no turret and no gun: the whole hull is the weapon. No body plan describes a sphere; casemate, a turretless hull that attacks straight ahead, is the nearest. The size is a judgement: it crushes main battle tanks, so it is bigger than one, but no source shows it twice their size.

armour.notes: Step 1 (the armour_map's Heavy vehicle) gives heavy; the batch registry note lifts it to super-heavy as one of the game's biggest units. It has nearly four times the Hunter Tank's health. Rifle and sniper hits do a quarter of their damage, explosive and fire hits half, rocket hits three quarters and cannon hits their full damage. Tempest Plating turns Charge into repairs; it is recorded as an ability rather than the self-repair model, since it heals only by using Charge up. Side-wide effects stay off: the Leading the Charge doctrine adds about a third more health to Dynasty vehicles and the Martial Plan a little rocket and explosive resistance.

sensors.notes: The wiki's sight figure is a little over half the Field Scout's, so short.

armament.name: Gimbal Roller
armament.summary: The Sphere's attack is its own body. Everything smaller than it, every soldier and the light and medium vehicles, is flattened as it rolls over them (the crush trait). What it cannot crush, heavy vehicles, hover units and buildings, it speeds up into and slams, a heavy blow at touching distance every couple of seconds; the build tooltip compares it to a wrecking ball rolling into enemy buildings. Since patch 1.7.0, in multiplayer, each slam also leaves the target Vulnerable: it takes nearly a third more damage from every source for a while. Ground targets only. Patch 1.8.0 fixed slams that could not reach some buildings, and patch 1.9.0 stopped it hurting uncrushable units just by rolling close to them. Coded as a melee weapon, since no family covers a ramming hull, with explosive damage from the game's Explosive type.

crew.notes: The Codex mentions a pilot who fires up the engines; one player rolls the ball and triggers the charge.

abilities.name: Tempest Engine
abilities.summary: The Sphere revs its engine for a moment, then shoots forward along a straight line at a burst of speed, flattening everything smaller in its path and slamming whatever is too big to crush. The Codex pitches it as the way to catch enemies who believe they are out of reach. A long wait follows each use.

abilities.name: Tempest Plating
abilities.summary: A perk unique to the Sphere: Tempest Charge that builds up on it, from Tempest fields or from enemy Charge weapons, is used up to repair it, a modest share of its health each time. It gives no protection from Overflow, which hurts the Sphere faster than the Plating can mend it.

on_death.notes: Since patch 1.7.0 a Demolitionist, the Dynasty's tier 3 heavy infantry in a powered exosuit with a wrecking hammer and a Voltaic gun, appears where the Sphere was destroyed and fights on. Doctrines bought for the whole side add more: with Manpower and a Plan running it also releases an Assault Gunner, and with Minefields it leaves an anti-tank mine.

strengths.why: Rolls over everything smaller than itself: every soldier, heavy infantry included, and light and medium vehicles, main battle tanks among them.
Nearly four times a main battle tank's health with resistances close to a tank's, so it soaks a great deal of fire while it rolls through a line.
Rams enemy buildings like a wrecking ball; the makers' showcase names breaking bases as its speciality.
The Tempest Engine charge closes the distance at once, flattening whatever lies on the line.

weaknesses.why: It harms only what it touches on the ground, so it has nothing against aircraft; the makers' showcase calls it vulnerable to the air.
The makers call it heavy and expensive: it costs about as much as three main battle tanks, so losing one hurts.
Heavy vehicles and hover units cannot be crushed, so against them it must slam each one in turn instead of rolling straight through.
The Tempest Engine has a long wait between uses, so a wasted charge leaves it without its gap-closer.

countered_by.why: Its ram reaches only ground targets, and the makers' showcase calls it vulnerable to the air.
Its armour takes the full force of Cannon hits and most of each Rocket hit, and it can strike back only by rolling into contact.

counters.why: Every soldier, heavy infantry included, dies outright when it rolls over them; the Codex says infantry stand no chance against it.
Crushes light and medium vehicles, main battle tanks among them, instead of trading shots; only heavy vehicles and hover units are spared.
Built to break bases: it rams buildings, defences and walls, and since patch 1.7.0 its slams leave them taking extra damage from the rest of the attack.

combos.why: An anti-air escort covers the threat its showcase names: aircraft, which it cannot touch.
Its slams leave the heavy vehicles it cannot crush Vulnerable, so anti-armour teammates finish them faster.

units.memorable: A giant gyroscopic wrecking ball that flattens soldiers and tanks alike, feeds on the Tempest Charge that cripples other vehicles, and drops a hammer-swinging Demolitionist when it finally breaks.
units.as_player: You are the ball: a huge, very tough T3 roller that kills by running things over. Steer into infantry and lighter vehicles to crush them, and slam heavy vehicles and buildings to leave them Vulnerable for your team. Q revs the Tempest Engine and launches you along a line, your one gap-closer, on a long wait. Nothing you have can touch aircraft, so bring anti-air friends; when you break, you play on as the Demolitionist who climbs out.

units.name: Enlightened

tier.basis: Spawned by the Resurrection Anchor, the Veti's construction yard, with no other tech needed; the wiki gives tier 1. The tier 3 Corral spawns them too, and Ambassador captures and Subjugated kills give more, but the Anchor route alone is enough.

cost_band.basis: Never bought: no route to an Enlightened costs credits. The Resurrection Anchor spawns one for free a little less than once a minute (a bit sooner since 2.0.0), the Corral somewhat sooner still and one more when it is first built, each Ambassador capture yields two, and each enemy soldier killed while Subjugated rises as one. Very low stands in for free (see fit_notes).

mobility.notes: Exactly the movement figure of the GDF Field Scout, the speed reference, on the wiki's scale. The wiki's prose still calls Enlightened weak and slow; the figure sets the band. The Refined Enlightenment doctrine makes them faster, and the Consecration a Sacrifice gives speeds up its receivers, never the thrall that is spent (both left off).

body.notes: A reanimated human body: by the Codex its brain is gone and a Tempest vine runs through its nerves instead. One soldier's size, in the wiki's standard infantry group.

armour.notes: Step 1 of the armour-class order decided: the infobox armour type Infantry maps to unarmoured. A little less health than the Field Scout. It takes full damage from Rifle attacks but only a quarter from Rocket and Cannon ones, and the Unit page rates infantry very weak to Fire and Sniper damage. As standard infantry it can be crushed by medium and heavy vehicles, and by the Unit page it drops prone under sustained fire at low health, taking half damage but unable to move until it gets up (see uncertain). The Refined Enlightenment doctrine gives it half again as much health (left off: a doctrine).

sensors.notes: It sees a little over half as far as the Field Scout (the wiki's figures), so short. No detection of its own; infantry spotting hidden units close by is game-wide. The wide high-ground sight and detection that its Sacrifice can give belong to the receivers' Augury perk (the Augur and the Veti Eye), not to the thrall.

armament.name: Melee
armament.summary: Fists: it pummels its target in a frenzy at touching distance, standing still to strike like every unit in the game. Each blow is weak and does Rifle-type damage, the kind meant for soldiers, which tanks mostly shrug off. It attacks only ground targets, never aircraft. Its Subjugating Attack passive marks enemy infantry it hits: a marked soldier cannot receive positive effects, and one that dies while marked rises as an Enlightened for the Veti. The Refined Enlightenment doctrine swaps the fists for the Phantom Caster.

armament.name: Phantom Caster
armament.summary: The Seeker's grenade weapon: it hurls unstable energy grenades that burst on impact and hurt everything in a small area around it, aimed at enemy soldiers and buildings by the makers' own Seeker line. It reaches a little over half as far as the Field Scout's rifle and fires only at ground targets, of which soldiers and buildings are recorded (see uncertain), with the same figures as the Seeker's copy. It keeps the Subjugating Attack passive, so infantry it hits are Subjugated as with the fists.
armament.condition: Only with Refined Enlightenment, level 4 of the Veti's Subjugation doctrine tree, bought during a match with credits and time: it replaces the Enlightened's fists, and the same doctrine gives them more health and speed.

crew.notes: One thrall, one player. It rides in Caretakers and Luminaries and garrisons Ascension Anchors (entering is a universal key); those carriers' own Garrison Enlightened buttons call idle thralls in, from twice as far since 2.0.0.

abilities.name: Sacrifice
abilities.summary: Ordered onto an area, the thrall is used up and Consecrates every friendly unit and building there: for a while they take a little less damage and move noticeably faster. Each receiver's own Consecrated perk adds more. Units on limited ammo (the Augur, Constellation, Gorgon, Luminary, Revenant, Subjugator and Vimana) get all missing ammo back and regain it faster; the Golem, Warden and War Ender mend over time; the Caretaker and Luminary gain a short-lived Repair Servitor, and an Enlightened sacrificed near the Ascended leaves a short-lived Combat Servitor; the Augur and Veti Eye see onto high ground and detect hidden units over a wide area; buildings with Consecrated Reaping earn credits. Other Veti units' shared Sacrificial Summons button sends the nearest idle Enlightened to do this onto them. Doctrines: Sacrificial Symbiosis makes Consecration last longer and has Enlightened sacrifice themselves when they die, and Sacred Sacrifice doubles its effects. Since 2.0.0 the Resurrection doctrine's Ascension Anchors consecrate a wider area, which the makers present as a stand-in for Sacrifice.

on_death.notes: Nothing of its own happens: it is simply gone. Effects from other units and from doctrines: Sacrificial Symbiosis has Enlightened sacrifice themselves automatically as they die; near a unit with Repair Servitor Progenesis (the Ambassador, Caretaker and Luminary) one leaves a Repair Servitor when it dies or sacrifices, and near one with Combat Servitor Progenesis (the Ascended, the Dominance Arc since 2.0.0, and the Dominance Anchor and Host Tower buildings) its death leaves a Combat Servitor; one the Shepherd has Empowered explodes as it dies, hurting enemy ground units nearby.

strengths.why: Its Sacrifice makes every allied Veti unit and building in the area take a little less damage and move noticeably faster for a while, and wakes each receiver's own Consecrated bonus.
Sacrifice hands Veti units that fire limited ammo, such as the Revenant's orbs, all their missing ammo and speeds up their refill.
Never bought: Veti buildings spawn them for free over time, each Ambassador capture yields two, and enemy soldiers killed while Subjugated rise as more.
Its punches Subjugate enemy soldiers: while marked they cannot be buffed, and if they die marked they rise as Enlightened for the Veti.

weaknesses.why: A little less health than the Field Scout and no armour against Rifle fire; the wiki calls Enlightened weak fighters that any armed unit dispatches easily.
It fights only with its fists at touching distance and must stand still to strike, so it has to walk through enemy fire before it can land a blow.
It sees only a little over half as far as the Field Scout.
Its punches deal Rifle-type damage, which the wiki rates good against infantry and which tanks mostly shrug off.

countered_by.why: Rifle fire meets no armour on it, so ordinary riflemen cut it down before its fists arrive; the wiki says any armed unit dispatches it easily.
Infantry take especially heavy losses from Fire weapons, by the Unit page.
Infantry take especially heavy losses from Sniper damage, by the Unit page.
Medium and heavy vehicles, the battle tanks among them, can crush standard infantry, and its punches barely hurt them.

counters.why: Infantry shrug off most Rocket and Cannon damage, so an enemy armed only with anti-tank weapons does little to a free thrall.
Enemy soldiers its punches Subjugate cannot receive positive effects, so an enemy buffer's boost does nothing for them while the mark lasts.

combos.why: The Revenant, a heavy anti-tank and anti-air soldier: by the makers' overview, sacrificing an Enlightened to it restocks its orbs.
The Augur, a recon specialist: by its build line, a nearby Enlightened's Sacrifice gives it far-reaching sight and refills its ammunition.
Veti carriers load Enlightened: the Caretaker spends one to plant an Ascension Anchor, which needs four and then eight more to rise a level, and the Luminary spends them on its own ranged Sacrifice.
The Shepherd can Empower nearby Enlightened so they explode as they die, hurting enemy ground units around them; no word-list or pattern link names that pairing.

units.memorable: A free, mind-wiped human thrall with feeble fists whose real worth is its death: it bursts itself to make the Veti forces around it tougher and faster.
units.as_player: You are free, frail fodder: punch enemy soldiers so the ones your team kills rise as more thralls, but your real job is Sacrifice. Walk into a knot of teammates and burst yourself to make them tougher and faster for a while, refilling ammo, mending or revealing for some of them, and then you are straight back on the buy screen.
